items.original_title: $P earnings were actually interesting, not really in terms actionable investments. But more on AI capex broadening, where deployments are happening, and what Jensen at $NVDA might envisioned with open weight model + GPU demand. - Everpure CEO stated that enterprises are increasingly building on-premises AI factories, stating: "The ROI for companies to buy their own GPU environments and run their own models is starting to come to the forefront." - "I'm talking about standard enterprises, regular finance organizations. A wide variety of organizations are starting to buy these AI factories for the purpose of running their own open weight models From "regular insurance companies, et cetera" - "One is they're starting to see that these open weight models are actually being able to provide good results, and they're doing so at a fraction of the cost of using the cloud for these workloads" "that the ROI for companies to buy their own GPU environments and run their own models is starting to come to the forefront" This type of broad industry transition would be heavily bearish as it threatens $ANT, OpenAI and frontier labs over the long term... And probably what Jensen saw things heading with $NVDA + additional GPU demand regardless of what frontier lab wins. However, I expect more of the open weight effort to collapse or see heavier regulation with how Washington + frontier labs were lobbying. - In regards to NAND prices dropping: "If prices come down slowly, I expect to see demand come up along with that" (Jevon) - LOL this part was hilarious and the same argument I was using for why qualification cycle players like in optics were so interesting. On data center slowdown potential: "So on the first part of it, remember, I mean, really, the thing that insulates us is we have such a small share going into the hyperscale market" "even in a down market, they’re going to spend a lot more than our current share amounts to", and their market capture goes up over time relative to overall TAM.

Markets appear to be wrongly interpreting Chinese eSSD cuts as deteriorating demand and NAND oversupply. Phison CEO commentary today + more context behind $SNDK / Kioxia selloff regarding Trendforce revisions: - "Pua attributed China's recent enterprise SSD demand slowdown to GPU shortages since November 2026" - "Without GPUs, additional purchases offer little value, prompting some companies to sell server components on the spot market to recover cash" (for context enterprise SSDs are growth driver for NAND) - "Chinese cloud giants nevertheless plan substantial GPU prepayments, temporarily tying up capital and delaying procurement of other components." - "the principal challenge in 2027 would be insufficient supply rather than weakening demand, with persistent AI shortages potentially prompting further procurement and inventory accumulation." Markets seemed to have wrongly interpreted this as demand destruction + pricing collapse. When Phison CEO attributed it to -> GPU shortages -> causing procurement timing mismatch -> Chinese CSPs needed capital for GPU prepayments, so liquidation in inventory (causing spot price volatility) -> timeline shift in order procurement TLDR: delayed procurement from GPU shortages. there were actual order cuts, but this is deferred procurement not structural demand weakening. Chinese CSPs needed capital for GPU prepayments so they liquidated other inventories in the meantime. Phison says its inventories are insufficient for anticipated 2027 demand and it's sees this as an opportunity for NAND accumulation. It's interesting the bottleneck in China migrated back to GPUs though.

True, I've looked at biotech, physical AI, cybersecurity, space, and others... But I still have conviction that optics is the most compelling opportunity. If you look at Elon Musk $SPCX (Mesh acquisition), $MRVL (Lumentum acqusition), Samsung Electronics photonics foundry push... SK Hynix CPO push + PIC IP acqusitions... it's endless. Private VCs are still heavily pouring funds into upcoming optical companies. Supply procurement is accelerating... from $SOI selling $1.2B in agreements, in a single quarter (from $25M revenue/quarter). To $COHR signing $20B in LTAs, to $LITE selling out of 2029 capacity. Actions about where the industry is heading is the biggest signal over valuations crashing. Even if you stress test aggregate capex slowdown or accelerator flood vs. grid constraint/permitting downside: - There's an economic incentive to improve GPU efficiency and power utilization. (eg. Lambda's CPO data suggests enough power savings to support ~4.5% more GPUs)... for power constrained DCs. - There's an economic incentive to reduce expensive HBM4 requirements in certain cases (eg. $MRVL estimating up to 30% savings through optical memory pooling)... for memory constrained inference. While for economic upside in these companies: -> Optical networking, and their upstream materials like substrates and lasers represent a relatively small fraction of total AI cluster BOM. -> At the same time, optical content goes up...while selling prices of that content rise nonlinearly as well (lasers 10x+ selling price from pluggable to CPO.) In terms of the future winners: - Many low end players eg. 400G/800G, module assemblers etc. don't capture the same scale in economics from the NPO/CPO transitions... compared to laser suppliers, fiber array suppliers, modulator suppliers, or companies in the ELS/optical engine stacks. - Tracking capacity expansion is also important... but US/China supply chain birufration will improve scarcity economics of Western players (eg. China optical transceiver bans past 3.2T) But even if aggregate AI capex slows, there's a strong economic incentive to accelerate optical deployments and to make every iota of compute more economically valuable. Visibility keeps increasing, demand keeps increasing, strategic value keeps increasing, while valuations crashed. NFA, but I'd personally, argue this is an opportunity. I'm hearing multiple things from industry executives: 1. Potential $NVDA employee exodus if Jensen doesn't come back soon. Many senior management and engineers can easily retire after Nvidia stock appreciation over the years. They don't need to continue working sitting on millions in equity. But they continued to work because Jensen was a visionary leader. Under new interim CFO (former CFO), it gives an excuse for that lot of people to finally quit soon. A pay bump or hiring $ARM CEO isn't going to change that. So you have generational talent leaving. 2. Loss of confidence in $NVDA future growth (Jensen was the moat). What I'm hearing is that Jensen understands heavily top-down architectures, and it's this magical discretionary element that doesn't get covered in media. When cuda, network, and $NVDA internal teams are arguing, Jensen made the final choices around heavily nuanced discretionary decision about where Nvidia + AI ecosystem ends up going: Then everyone followed. The supply chain, capital, agreements, and faith. You also can't suddenly replace the trust that local Taiwanese factories build with Jensen over the years if you bring in external CEOs, or even internal executives. It was transformational bet after bet after bet after bet that Jensen made until Nvidia became a former $5T+ company. 3. $NVDA is not that technologically far ahead of others. It's not a 5 year lead, but months ahead to a year in different areas. Jensen was accelerating all of that. Longer Jensen is gone, the longer Nvidia and its competitive ecosystem decays, beyond the current near-term roadmaps. Nvidia's greatest moat was Jensen Huang making high-stake architectural decisions and accelerating capital, suppliers, + the industry to rally around his vision. There's a massive loss of confidence in $NVDA with Jensen gone.

Elon Musk explains why SpaceX catching Starship achieves the "holy grail of rocketry," and can cut the cost of access to space by 100x: In 2025, SpaceX launched 2,200 tons to orbit, more than 80% of the global total. Elon Musk's goal with Starship is 1,000,000 tons to orbit per year, about 450x what SpaceX launched last year. Falcon 9 reuses its booster but throws away the upper stage on every flight. Starship is designed to bring back both. "We've had three booster catches, but this is the first ship catch, which means we've now at least proven that all parts of Starship can be flown to space and recovered in good enough shape to be reflown." "No one has ever taken a stage like that and created a truly reusable upper stage, and certainly not brought it back and had it land propulsively while being caught by giant chopsticks, which sounds like some kind of preposterous sci-fi book or something. But it's done." "Starship can drop the cost of access to space by a factor of 100... and achieve a mass to orbit rate that is in the million ton per year range." "This has been the holy grail of rocketry from the beginning, to have a fully reusable rocket system." "The Space Shuttle was partially reusable, but the main tank… was thrown away on every flight… The shuttle orbiter, the plane-like thing, would take something like nine months to refurbish between flights." "Whereas Starship is designed for complete reusability and to be reused immediately like an airplane. The booster lands, you can put another ship on top and take off immediately." "The net effect of this, to put it into economic terms, is a hundredfold reduction in the cost of access to space, and maybe even eventually a thousandfold reduction." "That's what's necessary in order to make life multiplanetary, in order to build a city on the Moon or Mars… You couldn't do it even if you had the whole budget of the United States government." Elon Musk and SpaceX have been working toward a fully reusable orbital rocket for more than two decades. Five days ago, they proved every part of Starship can fly to space and be recovered.

On Starship’s 15th flight last week, the Super Heavy booster correctly performed a safe abort when returning for a catch and ended its mission with a splashdown in the water off the coast of Starbase. Following splashdown, SpaceX recovery teams were immediately onsite to safe the area while our Environmental Health and Safety team worked to ensure any debris that washes onshore was recovered → https://t.co/ALNcWBQinC When we received reports of potential debris in Mexican territory, we immediately mobilized to send specialists to aid in identification and lead any cleanup work required, just as we did on Boca Chica Beach near Starbase. We continue to stay in contact with the Mexican government and are on standby to send support if authorities in Mexico tell us it is actually needed. Partners on the ground relayed that theyhave found very little debris in their sweeps of the beach, and the small amount they have found are not clearly from SpaceX operations. The majority of the social media posts online claiming widespread debris and damage are either outright fabrications or intentionally misleading. As repeatedly stated, independent tests conducted on materials inside Starship and the Super Heavy booster, including toxicity analyses, confirm they pose no chemical, biological, or toxicological risks. Starship is designed to be fully reusable, with future missions planning to return all hardware back to the launch site for catch and reuse. SpaceX is the only one, whether company or country, that has demonstrated this capability is now possible.

Now that we're close to 2027 it's a good idea to stress test downside scenarios where you have: 1. Capex cuts past 2028 2. Stranded Compute / DC Slowdowns 3. Finance deterioration (base case) 4. 2x+ rate hikes Working in parallel and see what happens with valuations of AI longs. If you see acceleration despite all 4, I'd argue that's an opportunity. > Next-gen of photonics is one of the rare segments with an extreme rise in optical content and ASPs that can offset aggregate capex cuts. Everyone’s moving into that space, including Elon Musk doing M&A, Marvell, Samsung and others with M&A… and we haven’t seen economic impact on emerging architectures even hit players from Celestial to Ayar + their suppliers yet. If we look at a scenario where there's excess GPUs but power constraints: We might see slowdown in aggregate accelerator/GPU/ASIC procurement, but your optical engines + light sources + switches players see acceleration. Especially as incentive to replace power inefficient networking... since different (cheap BOM) optical architectures improves GPU utilization or even HBM requirements. So value migrates to players more high-beta to architectural shifts. If Celestial projections are $500m -> $1B, and we expect -30% aggregate capex cuts, I'd argue we'd still see upward revisions from Celestial over the next 2 years. But financing with #3 matters a lot as seen with $AAOI dropping off of a $550M, vs. $COHR getting prepayments for capacity expansion from their customers. Companies that rely on external foundries might be less sensitive to #3 since they're not as capex intensive. On the other hand, companies in sectors have a lot of floating interest like certain Neoclouds, and require further financing might be the most impacted. > Legacy and specialty memory is a different cycle that markets conflate with AI capex. If consumer demand weakens but at the same time, players like Windbond exits DDR2, pricing durability is longer than markets expect. > Wafer/substrate procurement such as ABF, SOI, InP are low cost but large downstream destruction if not secured, so we’ll likely see acceleration here as seen with $NVDA earnings call. > qualification cycle players within bottlenecks remain very compelling, since first revenue in a large TAM, relative to MC is material to that company. If a company is valued at $400m then they get a $200m of orders, it's more asymmetrical to a certain company than a rounding error to a $50B incumbent revenue. _ There’s period of times where prices are dislocated from fundamentals from leveraged players getting wiped. I’d argue that time is now. I disagree with a lot of the stupid "it's over takes" but I agree it's a good idea to haircut future capex expectations and forward valuations due to financing tightening + macro. It's also good idea to see the nuances and stress test downside cases. But TLDR: I'd argue next phase of AI infrastructure is going to be increasingly disconnected from aggregate AI capex growth. I just personally wrote 4 things I'm using to stress test jointly some of the names I'm looking at, so I'm more comfortable waiting things out... despite seeing hedge funds getting liquidated left and right and overwhelming short positioning. I personally see acceleration in more narrow parts of the supply chain, while markets treat the entire AI trade as one. We'll see how things play out on longer horizons.
